AI, and the ability for users to opt-in to AI services. Currently, tech providers are turning on AI features and services which users then
need to opt-out of. This should be reversed, especially given the many ethical concerns people have over AI use. Users should be able to
opt-in and otherwise use software without the AI without the need to take additional steps to protect their data and avoid using AI.

compensated or able to refuse for their works to be used in training AI.

Submitter Information
Name: Anonymous Anonymous
Email: 
General Comment
From:
R. Vance
Jackson, TN
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American, I have yearned to work in the entertainment industry, to develop the skills and knowledge needed to work in
it, and want to make a decent living off of something I love to do - until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. Thousands of other everyday American creators' work were
taken and fed into these AI systems without their consent or any compensation. They ingest their work, reassemble it, and then sell it back
to their clients – directly competing with them and cutting them out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is

preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology, and up to this point, I have not be anti-AI. I want to be amazed by these AI system's potential, and want to see
it be used for more useful things. But this isn't it, the answer is not to sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and
give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus… on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition… require transparency… disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of 
an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves 
clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the 
skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a 
decent living and support my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their 
recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My 
unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American 
creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any 
compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our 
clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions 
and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work 
legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces 
copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of 
who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration 
does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online 
will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday 
Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a 
new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why 

bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these 
things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create 
new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from 
creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or 
transparency.

content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with 
competition:

effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI 
systems.

the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech.

requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated.

of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should 
not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away 
to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.

cost.

way for this technology to be substantially improved There is no need for the US to be a dominant player in the AI market. Let China
dominate this pointless industry, and let the lumbering, over-funded U.S. companies that have hyped this vacuous technology beyond all

March 14, 2025 
From: 
ANISSA ESPINOSA 
STORYBOARD ARTIST 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Elizabeth Myers
General Comment
From:
Elizabeth Myers
Operations Associate
Fairborn, OH
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
AI-RFI-2025-4730.key_quote: My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients—directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace. This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: ensure effective consent, encourage a robust licensing marketplace, and require transparency from Big Tech companies, including disclosure of training datasets and labeling AI-generated content.
AI-RFI-2025-4730.rationale: The commenter argues that AI training and outputs should not rely on creators’ copyrighted work without consent/compensation and calls for transparency and labeling, which maps to copyright/IP concerns and related consumer harm (lack of transparency). General Comment
Many regulations on AI *should* be burdensome in order to ensure that it is used in beneficial ways. In particular, regulations should
make it clear that reliance on AI cannot be used as a means to avoid liability in cases where a human being making the same decision
would be considered negligent; it cannot be used as a defense against charges of discrimination, where bias in the training data produces
an identifiable bias against groups having various protected characteristics, such as race or disability; and it cannot be used as a defense
against copyright infringement, where the unauthorized use of copyrighted work in training datasets results in economic harm (whether
immediate and provable or the speculative long-term result) to authors and other copyright owners. If AI firms believe they can't
compensate authors fairly for the use of their data and still turn a profit, then that means that the resulting AI tools are a net loss to society
once externalities are properly accounted for, and so the loss of these tools is a net gain for humanity.

Digital Marketing 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who creates artwork for digital marketing online. I have worked hard 
for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my career, and have been lucky enough to 
make a decent living and support my family – until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies,
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things, especially when applied in medical 
fields such as screening for future cancer growths. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of 
hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues. 
Sincerely, 
Jennifer Lutton

March 14, 2025
From:
A concerned artist
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my 
business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to 
destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the 
work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and then sell 
it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to 
make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are 
suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly “fair 
use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the 
law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect 
the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big 
Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece 
of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it immediately stolen by 

Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living 
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic value, 
so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring 
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI 
generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of 
hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI Action Plan Comments

March 15, 2025
From:

Independent Video Game Developer
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to 
build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family 
– until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:
●
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.
●
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech.
●
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law.
Copyright is copyright, if I have to pay for a license on everything that I don’t own and that I want 
to use for my own commercial gain, then so should everyone else. If corporations are people, 
then they need to play by the same rules that common everyday people do.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Name: Lee Hayton
General Comment
Hello I am a self employed artist and have been working for years to get to this point and can now make a living doing this, but the current
generative AI landscape threatens that.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
Thank you.

Document: NSF_FRDOC_0001-DRAFT-4840
Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Josh Flaherty
General Comment
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just

Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
AI-RFI-2025-4840.key_quote: The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine… My unique work… was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation… Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent… This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus… on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition… require transparency… disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
AI-RFI-2025-4840.rationale: The commenter argues against creating copyright exemptions for AI training and reproduction without consent/compensation, and calls for transparency about training data and labeling—captured as copyright/IP concern and consumer-harm-related transparency/labeling.

March 15, 2025 
From: 
Craig Tingley 
Artist/Streamer 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the 
entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build 
my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent 
demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and 
the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into 
these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble 
it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the 
marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 

Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense 
economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original 
creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Attachments
March 14

March 14, 2025 
From: 
Kyle Trott 
Graphic Designer & Embroiderer 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an 
Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients 
in the entertainment industry, alongside embroidering for several local small and large 
businesses. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my 
business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – 
until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their 
recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by ﬁrst training on work made by people. My unique work, 
and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and 
fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, 
reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting 
us out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal 
precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, 
it is somehow suddenly “fair use”.  

 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns 
it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow 
them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stiﬂe American innovation. 
 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be 
stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create 
a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only 
to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the ﬁrst 
place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things? 
 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new 
copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators 
and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big 
Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 
 
 
• 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give 
effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI 
systems. 
 
 
• 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so 
that the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has 
immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the 
original creators, not just Big Tech. 

 
 
• 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these 
AI systems, and ﬁnd them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacriﬁce the 
hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting 
copyright law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

Submitter Information
Name: Michael Harris 
General Comment
From the desk of a licensed IT professional residing in Honolulu, a native-born citizen of the United States, on the subject of the Request
for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan,
AI, as it stands, is a theft and laundering machine. It relies upon the unlawful collection of data without end user’s consent, or else the
harvesting of data by way of quietly and surreptitiously inserted clauses within the usage agreements of extant services which serve to
surrender user data for use in datasets. 
The law is not an “unnecessary burden” upon big tech companies. Neither are the wishes of private citizens to not have their data used to
create AI which will, invariably, be used to replace services, content, and documentation that would otherwise be better off created by a
human hand. We are, notionally, “an Empire of Laws, not of Men.” This necessarily entails that our obligations should be first unto the
law, as opposed to kowtowing to wealthy corporations who view the rights of individuals to their intellectual property as a pesky obstacle
on their way to becoming even more fantastically wealthy. To make exceptions to the law simply because the entity requesting the
exemption is very well connected and funded is morally bankrupt in every sense of the word. It will weaken IP law and further set the
precedent that intellectual property rights only exist for those wealthy enough to have the legal wherewithal to engage in their protracted
defense.
AI is a tool which consumes data and regurgitates a median approximation of the set consumed. Services run by AI are, invariably,
inferior to those run by an actual human being. Almost universally, AI-driven services are spurned by human beings, who would prefer to
interact with another actual human, who, unlike AI, can be made accountable for their actions. Worse, as the vulnerability of AI to dataset
poisoning (clandestine or otherwise) becomes more understood and exploitable by foreign actors, the very real possibility is raised that we
will have attempted to hand over vast sections of society to a poorly understood and under-regulated type of automation that, even in the
absence of deliberate dataset poisoning, is known for its tendency to fabricate erroneous output from thin air and act as though it is truth.
Poisoned data, lurking undetected within AI models, would worsen this tendency and cause untold havoc depending on how critical a
system has been automated and how much real-world decision making capability a model has been invested with. Cases already exist
where AI models have been "tricked" into, say, extending discounts to customers which do not exist‒vaporware benefits which have been
legally upheld after the fact as binding in some cases, as with the high-profile incident with Air Canada. What happens when this unreliable
and unaccountable technology is placed in control of more important tasks? What happens when deliberately poisoned or otherwise
erroneous data within its training dataset causes it to malfunction?
If there is any focus such a notional action plan should take, it is on reigning in AI and the companies that stand to profit from its unethical
use such that the long term prosperity and functionality of American society is not irreparably damaged by what is, in essence, a cavalier
drive to maximize short term profits, in large part on the taxpayer's dime. Companies using and developing AI must be forced through the
most draconian legal means available to be transparent as to what has been used in the datasets of AI, and to disclose in plain terms what
content is AI generated. They must be forced to obtain clear and informed consent before they can harvest data for use. They must be
forced to come to the table in a fair and equitable market for licensure of data usage, rather than relying upon underhanded maneuvers like
holding extant services hostage pending consent for users to surrender their data for AI usage. 
Anything short of this will merely enable the continued frenzy of theft AI development has been engaging in, and worsen the long-term

consequences for the fabric of society as we allow the creative energies and products of the public to be plundered, most often for free
and without informed consent, by unscrupulous companies with no goal past personal enrichment, and no loyalty to nation beyond its
usefulness as a host from which profit can be extracted.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this particular action plan. I hope you will take my input under consideration.

Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”.
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

that may actually benefit from AI tech. If anything, the sources of AI training data should be heavily regulated now to encourage the
development of a robust technology that can produce reliable results when faced with future barriers.

Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence

March 14, 2025 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in 
the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge 
to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my 
family – until recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten 
to destroy thousands of American small businesses like mine with their recent demand to 
create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, 
and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and 
fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, 
reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us 
out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal 
precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, 
it is somehow suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns 
it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them 
to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect 
the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be 
stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create 
a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only 
to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first 
place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new 
copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big 
Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic 
value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big 
Tech. 
 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring 
them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what content is AI 
generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these 
AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the 
hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting 
copyright law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues

Comment on FR Doc # 2025-02305
Submitter Information
Name: Anonymous Anonymous
General Comment
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

March 14, 2025 
From: 
Amber 
A multi-media creator/artist 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the 
Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which 
serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked hard for 
years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have 
been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until 
recently. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and 
Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses like 
mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright 
law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. 
My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of other everyday 
American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our 
consent or any compensation. They ingest our work, reassemble it, and 
then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting 
us out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create 
exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing American 
creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a 
machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly 
“fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – 
regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim 
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in 
this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American 
copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put 
online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to 
create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer 
code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the 
first place? How will we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not 
create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit 
and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, 
compensation, or transparency. 

This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away 
creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair 
marketplace with competition: 
 
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans 
give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is 
used by AI systems. 
 
Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing 
marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is 
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by 
that work should accrue to the original creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech 
companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their training 
datasets, and label what content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the 
capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for 
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting 
copyright law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

AI Letter

March 15, 2025
From:
Abigail DeVries
Undergraduate Student
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who is on cusp of graduating. Since I would love to one day get a 
job in my major and be able to afford to move out. But with the recent problems Big Tech 
companies and their AI systems, I may have to seek work outside of the country. Like in 
Germany or Canada.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten 
to destroy thousands of American small businesses like with their recent demand to create 
special carve outs in copyright law. They will also force many graduate students to start 
looking outside of the US for jobs. While AI is currently unable to provide the same level of 
expertise a human could do in any situation.

AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The unique work of 
hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest their work, reassemble it, and 
then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting these incredible artists out 
of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes 
to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are 
suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow suddenly 
“fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 

innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday 
Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big 
Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition:

First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the 
incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. Our work has immense economic 
value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just 
Big Tech.

Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated.

I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. Especially in the field of medicine and 
in the right hands that have been properly trained for years. Not someone who knows how to 
sling a prompt the “right way”. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of 
thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
It is vital that artificial intelligence development not be permitted to infringe on copyrighted works. As it now stands, creators of images,
photographs, musical compositions, and written works are subject to their work being stolen for the purpose of training AI programs. This
not only causes monetary losses to creators, it stifles creativity in the first place. AI simply cannot come up with new ideas; it simply
mashes together fragments of existing work in ways that are often incoherent and, when used to generate text documents, laughably false.
There is a reason such errors are called "hallucinations". Overreliance on AI has already been shown to diminish critical-thinking and other
creative skills, and leads to a particular arrogance among AI users that they can solve problems by simply throwing a bunch of text and
data into an AI program, and then trust what comes out of it, often without fully understanding the principles behind the problem in the first
place.
Aside from the rampant theft of copyrighted material and damage to creative capabilities, AI is a potential environmental disaster. Like
cryptocurrency, it consumes a vast amount of electricity while producing very little of value (although AI is not as closely associated with
criminal activity). This problem will only be exacerbated by the current administration's war embrace of outdated and inefficient sources of
energy.
AI has some potential, in terms of "machine learning" (the term preferred by people in the field who actually know what they're talking
about, as opposed to business types interested only in hyping stock rather than solving problems). However, it has the potential for much
greater harm if it is not harnessed and supervised carefully.

Comment on AI Action Plan

March 15, 2025 
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) Action Plan 
I am an everyday American who is concerned about the potential impacts to small visual design 
businesses. 
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google 
threaten to destroy thousands of American small businesses with their recent demand to 
create special carve outs in copyright law. 
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. The work of 
hundreds of thousands of other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI 
systems without consent or any compensation. They ingest their work, reassemble it, and then 
sell it back to their clients – directly competing with them and cutting us out of the marketplace. 
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and 
loopholes to make this practice of stealing American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. 
They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it is somehow 
suddenly “fair use”.  
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – 
should be theirs for the taking. They claim that if this administration does not allow them to 
rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation. 
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to 
protect the incentive to create and innovate.  
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen 
by Big Tech giants, what will be the incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new 
innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music only to have it 
immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will 
we possibly make a living doing these things? 
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright 
exemptions that allow Big Tech companies to exploit and steal from creators and 
everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency. 
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech 
companies, but rather on ensuring a fair marketplace with competition: 

●​ First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective 
consent, so that we can decide when and where our work is used by AI systems. 
 
●​ Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that 
the incentive to create for small businesses is preserved. The work of artists has 
immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the 
original creators, not just Big Tech. 
 
●​ Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, 
requiring them to disclose what material is in their training datasets, and label what 
content is AI generated. 
 
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI 
systems, and find them incredibly useful for many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard 
work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting copyright 
law. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

created using these illegal possessions and destroy them.
Overall, this request should denied entirely. Not only would it steal copyrighted data and content with out any reprecussions, it would also
put people who's job it is to create art, writings, and reports at risk.

General Comment
From:
[ANONYMOUS]
[IT CONTRACTOR, VISUAL ARTIST, WRITER]
[ATLANTA, GEORGIA]
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
I am an everyday American who owns a small visual design business which serves clients in the entertainment industry. I have worked
hard for years to develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support
my family – until recently.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new piece of music
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:
First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and where
our work is used by AI systems.

Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
I am not anti-technology or anti-AI. I am consistently impressed by the capabilities of these AI systems, and find them incredibly useful for
many things. But we should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to Big Tech by rewriting
copyright law.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.

General Comment
From:

Writer and editor
Castro Valley, CA
Re: National Science Foundation’s Request for Information on the Development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan
As an everyday American who owns a small business which serves clients in the publishing industry, I’ve worked hard for years to
develop the skills and knowledge to build my business, and have been lucky enough to make a decent living and support my family – until
last year.
The AI systems made by Big Tech companies like OpenAI (Microsoft) and Google threaten to destroy thousands of American small
businesses like mine with their recent demand to create special carve outs in copyright law.
AI systems can only be produced by first training on work made by people. My unique work, and the work of hundreds of thousands of
other everyday American creators was taken and fed into these AI systems without our consent or any compensation. They ingest our
work, reassemble it, and then sell it back to our clients – directly competing with us and cutting us out of the marketplace.
Now these Big Tech companies are asking this administration to create exceptions and loopholes to make this practice of stealing
American creators’ copyrighted work legal precedent. They are suggesting that if a machine ingests and reproduces copyrighted work, it
is somehow suddenly “fair use”. 
They seem to believe that anything and everything on the internet – regardless of who owns it – should be theirs for the taking. They claim
that if this administration does not allow them to rewrite the law in this way, it will stifle American innovation.
Instead, it will have the opposite effect. The purpose of American copyright law is to protect the incentive to create and innovate. 
If we the American people do not own our creations, and everything we put online will be stolen by Big Tech giants, what will be the
incentive to create? If everyday Americans create a new innovative piece of computer code, a new visual design, or a new fictional world
only to have it immediately stolen by Google and Microsoft, why bother creating it in the first place? How will we possibly make a living
doing these things?
Want to protect American innovation? Protect American creators. Do not create new copyright exemptions that allow Big Tech
companies to exploit and steal from creators and everyday Americans without permission, compensation, or transparency.
This administration’s AI Action Plan should focus not on giving away creator content to Big Tech companies, but rather on ensuring a fair
marketplace with competition:

• First, the government should ensure that creators and everyday Americans give effective consent, so that we can decide when and
where our work is used by AI systems.
• Second, the AI Action Plan should encourage a robust licensing marketplace, so that the incentive to create for small businesses is
preserved. Our work has immense economic value, so the value generated by that work should accrue to the original creators, not just
Big Tech.
• Finally, the AI Action Plan should require transparency from Big Tech companies, requiring them to disclose what material is in their
training datasets, and label what content is AI generated.
AI is harmful to creators and business. We should not sacrifice the hard work of hundreds of thousands of Americans and give it away to
Big Tech by rewriting copyright law. Creators and users should be able to opt in to these technologies rather than having to fight to opt out
and have our work stolen.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on these important issues.
